column2: How do I search for a Finnish ancestor in HisKi?
column3: “🔍 Online archives…” → “Finland” → “📋 Copy the name and open”: HisKi opens; choose the parish and paste the name. First names are in Swedish or Finnish there (Johan / Juho, Maria / Maija). Then copy the table of results, then “🔗 Paste a link”: each line becomes a record to tick (baptism → birth and baptism, burial → death and interment). A marriage is never added by itself: it stays in the source.

column2: How do I find a trial in London (Old Bailey, 1674-1913)?
column3: “🔍 Online archives…” → “United Kingdom” → “Old Bailey Online”: the search opens with their name. Copy the text of the trial (or save the page), then “⤒ Import”: the app reads the reference (t17800628-33 = 28 June 1780), the crime, the verdict and the sentence, translated, and suggests an event “Defendant (or Victim, Witness) at the trial” with the source.

column2: Why don’t Ancestry, MyHeritage, Filae or ScotlandsPeople appear any more?
column3: Because “Free only” is ticked at first: the paying sites are hidden. Untick it (in “Search the Internet”, in the “🔍 Search the online archives” window or in Settings → Appearance → Search the Internet) to see them: they always come at the end, with the “PAYING” badge and a sentence saying what is paid for. Geneanet stays shown: it is free, only its Premium part is paying (“PARTLY PAYING” badge).

column2: How do I see the addresses of a census on a plan?
column3: Lists → Surveys (“Plan” tab) or a village record: the households are placed from their address, for the year of your choice. Old street names and vanished streets are drawn by hand; favourite base maps are chosen in Settings → Appearance.

column2: How do I prepare a field trip?
column3: Lists → Field tours: the stops (town halls, cemeteries, archives), the logistics and the practicalities of each. Lists → Archive visit planner for the references to consult.

column2: How do I note a cadastral parcel (a plot of land, a meadow, the ancestors’ house)?
column3: Lists → Places and houses → “🗺 Cadastre” → “＋ Add a parcel”. Choose the commune, write the section (“AB”, “B”) and the number as they appear on the deed, the register or the plan, then “🔍 Search”: the outline, the area (in m² and ares) and the number come by themselves. You can also “🗺 Click on the map”. Then link the owners and occupants (with a role and dates: “from 1834 to 1872”), the house from the House tool, deeds of sale or division, an extract from the register, the scanned plan, a source. The parcel appears on the person’s record (“🗺 Owner of…”), the house’s and the village’s.

column2: What can be retrieved from the cadastre, and under what licence?
column3: Everything the app fetches is free of rights and free of charge, with no account or key: today’s cadastral plan (DGFiP, published by IGN: “Parcellaire Express”, Licence Ouverte 2.0 — you may reuse it by citing “IGN / DGFiP”) for the outline, the section, the number and the area (IGN’s API Carto, with the Géoplateforme as a backup); the nearest present-day address (Base Adresse Nationale, Licence Ouverte 2.0); sales since 2020 (“Demandes de valeurs foncières”, Etalab, Licence Ouverte 2.0: date, price, kind of land, never a name). It is your computer that asks, with only the commune, the section and the number (or a point on the map): no person’s name is sent. The answers are kept for 30 days. NOT free: the names of today’s owners (land files, restricted) and, often, the images of old plans held by the archives (conditions specific to each department).

column2: How do I note who inherited what (will, division, probate inventory)?
column3: Lists → Media and documents → “🏠 Inheritances and estates” → “＋ New deed”. Choose the kind (will, division, probate inventory, gift, sale between heirs, marriage contract with the dowry, estate declaration), the date as on the deed, the notary, the office, the place, the reference and the source; a probate inventory already noted can be linked too. In “The people”: ⭐ the deceased (or the donor), ★ the heirs and beneficiaries, ☆ the others (witnesses, guardian…), each with their role (heir, legatee, usufructuary…). In “The property”: a house (House tool), a parcel (Cadastre), a family object, or land, a sum of money, furniture written by hand, with the value, the share (“one third”, “in usufruct”) and the “To whom” boxes (nothing ticked: to all the heirs). The images of the deed go through the image window. What you note follows the deeds: the app gives no legal advice.

column2: How do I see the chain of owners of a house or a family object?
column3: Open the house (House tool, “🏠 House” tab → “Chain of owners”) or the object (Lists → Family objects → Edit): a timeline arranges, year after year, each deed that passes it on (from whom → to whom, the share, the notary); for an object, the “Transmission” steps noted on the object are mixed in. “＋ New deed for this house” creates the deed with the property already chosen. On a person’s record, the “🏠 What they received / passed on” block (Settings → Appearance → record blocks) sums up their inheritances.

column2: What is the division diagram of an inheritance?
column3: On a deed’s page (Lists → “🏠 Inheritances and estates”), “🔀 Division diagram” draws as a flow who gives what property to whom: by value when each item has a sum in the same currency, otherwise one item = one share (divided equally). “📊 Edit in My diagrams” takes it into the diagram editor to dress it up or export it. Next to a sum in livres, sous or francs, “≈ … € today” gives an order of magnitude (the calculation of the 🪙 Old money converter, which opens with a click on the 🪙 next to the sum), not an exact value.

column2: How do I see the parcels on the map?
column3: Map → “▦ Parcels” switch: today’s cadastral plan is shown over the background (zoom in close enough), with your parcels in blue (a click opens one). “📍 Parcel here” then a click on the map: the parcel at that spot, which you can add to your list. The “Cadastre parcels (IGN)” background also exists in the list of backgrounds (Overlay mode), and the “▦ Parcels” switch in a village’s address plan.

column2: How do I get the Napoleonic plan (old cadastre) of a commune?
column3: The first cadastre (called “Napoleonic”, around 1810-1850) and its registers are in the departmental archives: the parcel’s page gives the link to the department archives’ website and a search on FranceArchives (links without guarantee: sites change). Many departments show them online; the conditions for reuse vary from one department to another (often: free personal use, publication on request). Download or photograph the section, then on the parcel’s page “＋ Align an old plan”: the image goes into the media, and you click 2 points (or more, which is better: the church, a crossroads, the corner of a house) on the image and then at the same spot on today’s map. The plan is laid on the Map with its transparency (“My old map”), and it is linked to the parcel. The old number is noted in “Old number”.

column2: The parcel in my deed no longer exists in today’s cadastre?
column3: Parcels have often been divided, merged or renumbered (land consolidation). Note the old number (“B 245 (1834)”) and the locality name, without an outline, or look on the map for today’s parcel at the same spot. “↻ Read online again” updates the outline and area of a parcel already noted.

column2: A foreign place is not offered?
column3: The cities of the world are prepared once at first launch (a few minutes). A place that cannot be found can always be typed by hand.

column2: How do I make a maze, and look for ancestors in it?
column3: Open the Game, choose “🌀 Maze” in “Game”. Set the shape (square, hexagons, round, heart, tree, France, star), the size, the corridors (long corridors, many dead ends, balanced, all random), the loops, the start and the finish, then the look (line, hedges, stones, parchment, colours of the walls, the floor and the path). The preview follows each setting; “🎲 Another one” changes the seed (the same seed gives the same maze again). In 3, “Things to go and find”: up to 12 ancestors, places, events, houses or photos from your genealogy, in the order you like, from the oldest to the most recent, or “Climb back up your line” (Sosa 16 → 8 → 4 → 2); the exit can stay closed until everything has been collected. Living people and confidential records are never in it.

column2: How do I play the maze with several people?
column3: In “4 · The players”, add up to 4 players. “Each in turn”: everyone goes through the same maze and the times are compared. “All at once”: a race, with the arrows, W A S D, I J K L and the numeric keypad. You can also drag your piece with the mouse or a finger. Space pauses, H gives a hint (a few yellow dots), “👁 Show the solution” draws the path. At the end: the time, the steps, the stops, and ↗ the record of each ancestor met.

column2: How do I print a maze for children?
column3: In the game: “🖨 Print” gives the maze on one page, the list of stops, and the solution on a second page. “⤓ Export ▾” saves it as a PNG image or an SVG drawing, with or without the solution. Your favourite settings are kept in “💾 Saved settings” (with four “Ready-made sets”: Easy for children, Big challenge, Looking for the ancestors, Tour of France’s villages).

column2: How do I play “Guess Who?” with my ancestors?
column3: Open the Game, choose “🕵️ Ancestors’ Guess Who?” in “Game”. Choose the people (your Sosa ancestors, one generation, a person’s ancestors or the whole genealogy) and the number of portraits. An ancestor is hidden: ask questions (“Is it a woman?”, “Born before 1800?”, “Was she a ploughman?”, “Born in Auch?”, “On your father’s side?”); the portraits that no longer fit are greyed out by themselves. Click a portrait to set it aside yourself. “🎯 I’ll make a guess” when you think you know (a wrong guess counts as 2 questions). With two players, each has their hidden ancestor, drawn at random or chosen in secret by the other. Living people and confidential records are never in the games.

column2: How do I play Portrait Memory?
column3: Open the Game, choose “🃏 Portrait Memory”. Choose the kind of pairs (portrait ↔ name, person ↔ village of birth, person ↔ occupation, person ↔ year of birth) and the number of pairs (6 to 24). You turn over two cards; a pair found stays visible and the same player plays again. From 1 to 4 players, with the timer and the number of moves. With the keyboard: arrows then Enter or Space.
